..
Issued at 348 PM CDT Mon Oct 12 2026

Windy conditions continue across the area today, with a surface low 
over eastern South Dakota and a surface high off the Gulf Coast 
enhancing the pressure gradient over much of the central CONUS. 
Gusts are expected to cap out around 35-40 mph under a well-mixed 
boundary layer through the remainder of the afternoon and evening. 
Temperature-wise, it is very hot (for October), with daytime highs 
hovering around the high 80s/low 90s under strong, sustained WAA at 
the lowest levels of the atmosphere. As the surface low continues 
progressing off towards the northeast, a cold front (presently over 
southeastern NE) is projected to sag down across northwest 
MO/northeast KS through the overnight. Along the boundary, ongoing 
moist advection could contribute to isolated/scattered showers, 
especially across northwest MO. However, these probabilities remain 
on the lower end (~10-15%). Global guidance has progressively 
shifted its solution for the cold front southward, aligning better 
with short term guidance and increasing confidence in a cooler 
temperature forecast for portions of northwest MO/northeast KS. 
Highs in the high 70s/low 80s will be a stark contrast to the high 
80s/low 90s south of the US-36 corridor, where the temperature 
forecast will once again approach daily records and heat indices 
look to hover around the triple digits. South of the boundary, 
sustained south/southwesterly winds will transport warm, moist air 
across much of the forecast area, with dewpoints rising into the low 
70s. This will contribute to a corridor of moderately unstable air 
(MUCAPE as high as 2500 J/kg) developing during the daytime. By the 
afternoon, there is a low (15-30%) for showers/storms to develop as 
the cap gradually erodes. However, the greatest chances (60-80%) 
reside during the evening, when a strengthening LLJ and shortwave 
trough to the west invigorates synoptic-scale ascent. Effective bulk 
shear remains strong around 40-50 kts during this time period, which 
favors the development of strong/severe storms. However, mid-level 
lapse rates remain marginal at around 6.5 degC/km. The most 
favorable corridor for severe development will be for areas 
along/south of the boundary, with threats for damaging wind and hail 
up to quarters in the strongest storms. The severe threat will 
diminish through the night as capping returns, but residual elevated 
MUCAPE could maintain strong/severe storms through the overnight 
period. Also of note is enhanced PWATs with the environment,
increasing the risk of minor localized flooding if storms train
over the same locations.

Convective activity will help to push the boundary further south on 
Wednesday, but guidance continues to deviate on exactly how far 
south the boundary will sag. Recent CAMs indicate varied solutions 
on the continuation of shower/storm activity during the 
morning/early afternoon on Wednesday. Depending on the longevity of 
this activity, how far south the boundary progresses during the day, 
and the presence of cloud debris inhibiting daytime heating, a 
continued risk for strong thunderstorms exists on Wednesday. 
However, with recent CAM guidance keeping the most favorable 
corridor for development further south over the Ozark Plateau, the 
risk for continued severe across the area is limited.

PoPs continue through at least Thursday before an upper-level trough 
situated over the Western CONUS lifts towards the Great Lakes and 
synoptic high pressure builds in behind it. A strong cold front will 
drape down across the forecast area by the end of the week, 
significantly lowering temperatures in its wake and keeping us much 
cooler and drier going into the weekend compared to the previous few 
days. Guidance continues to indicate the potential of reaching lows 
in the 30s by Friday evening/Saturday morning, increasing confidence 
in seeing our first frost/freeze across the area. Through the 
remainder of the weekend, guidance generally agrees on the gradual 
progression of an upper-level ridge eastward over the central CONUS, 
with surface high pressure sliding off towards the OH Valley and 
shifting winds out of the south. With this shift of winds towards 
the south, the forecast will warm slightly by the end of the 
forecast period, with temperatures in the 60s/70s.
